source.title: Beyond Losses Reweighting: Empowering Multi-Task Learning via the Generalization Perspective
source.authors: Hoang Phan; Lam C. Tran; Q. Tran; Ngoc N. Tran; Tuan Truong; Qi Lei; Nhat Ho; Dinh Q. Phung; Trung Le

record.tranche_reason: Extends sharpness-aware training to multi-task learning and reports train and test performance; it does not directly test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports multi-task classification and scene-understanding results, plus training/test accuracy curves. Its comparisons of aggregation strategies and cited prior results are not rows. No result tests arbitrary-label memorization, architecture comparisons, optimizer or batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flatness–generalization relationship to design a multi-task training method and evaluates its performance. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness ranking of generalization gaps or any other listed version. Its bounds concern perturbed empirical loss plus complexity terms, rather than the claimed empirical ranking.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that their sharpness-aware framework improves multi-task performance and generalization, supported by higher test accuracy with similar training accuracy. Improvements are not universal across individual metrics; for example, F-MGDA reduces NYUv2 segmentation mIoU.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies a sharpness-aware, gradient-decomposed training procedure to multi-task learning; it does not use random-label memorization experiments or directly reproduce a listed version.
record.method_sensitivity: Perturbation radius ρ changes the accuracy response: the paper reports stability from ρ = 0.5 and saturation of improvement when ρ ≥ 1.5 (Supplementary D.3), but these values are used for method sensitivity rather than as direct claim-version results.

fits_no_version.finding: On three two-task image datasets, the proposed sharpness-aware training method improves test accuracy over ERM from approximately epoch 20, while both methods attain similar training accuracy approaching 100% from approximately epoch 50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed multi-task sharpness-aware training procedure improves held-out accuracy without improving training accuracy in these experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: D.4–D.8 report flatter test-loss surfaces, greater tolerance to Euclidean weight perturbations, and lower training sharpness for the proposed method than ERM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed training procedure produces solutions with greater measured flatness and perturbation robustness than ERM in the tested multi-task settings.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision
record.problems: The train and test accuracy comparisons relevant to the generalization statement are shown as curves without exact values in the text. The evidence is for multi-task benchmarks and does not isolate the specific conditions or measurements in the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for each task or dataset: the text summarizes the Figure 12 result across all tasks and datasets, and Figure 13 training accuracy similarly describes both methods collectively. Additional figures report sharpness, gradient norms, calibration, robustness, and conflict, but do not directly measure a claim version's specified generalization gap or intervention.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting and held-out performance compared with natural labels under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on training-set size, augmentation, or weight decay.

Whether magnitude-aware weight-perturbation tolerance ranks train–test gaps among comparably fitted networks, and whether it ranks them better than norm- and margin-based measures. Adaptive SAM training, Euclidean perturbation robustness, and sharpness curves do not establish these comparisons.
Retraining after removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The additional sharpness and robustness findings are already declared in rows_left_out. Neither these findings nor the generalization bounds justify a verdict on V7. The cannot_determine row states concern applicability to the listed versions, not whether the reported method improvements occurred.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same recipe.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization comparisons.
Large versus small batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness comparisons among similarly low-training-loss networks and ranking of train-test gaps.
Removing the training examples most associated with memorized labels.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Compared proposed sharpness-aware multi-task method with ERM training.
rows.measure: Test accuracy across tasks and datasets
rows.value: The flat-based method outperforms ERM on all tasks and datasets from the 20-th epoch (curves in Figure 12; no exact values stated in the text).
rows.note: Authors describe the comparison across all tasks and datasets; plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: The reported test-accuracy improvement is supported by D.7, but this is the proposed method's performance against ERM, not a result on a listed version. Exclude it from claim-evidence rows and retain under fits_no_version. It also combines six task-by-dataset comparisons.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Compared training accuracy after ERM and proposed sharpness-aware multi-task training.
rows.value: Training accuracy scores of both methods are similar and reach ≈ 100% from 50-th epoch.
rows.note: The authors interpret the similar training accuracy alongside improved test accuracy as generalization enhancement.
rows.check: D.7 supports similar training accuracy approaching 100%, but natural-label training accuracy alone tests no listed version. This is a companion method-performance result; retain under fits_no_version rather than claim-evidence rows.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
